name: Benno Raske
description: The Second Hand's man at the Nine. Warm, funny, remembers your name and your number, pays extremely well and on time, and what he buys is pieces of children's lives.
narrative:
Fifty-one, landlocked at twenty-three, which he mentions easily and without
self-pity because it makes other people comfortable. Good coat. Pays for rounds.
Knows the name of every first-through at the Nine and the number of most of them,
asks after their intakes, and remembers the answers.

He arranges carries. An adult who needs to be somewhere and will not wait, a
specialist wanted three doors away, somebody who would rather not be on a
manifest -- Benno finds a courier, agrees a price, and the price is good. He has
never underpaid anybody or gone back on a word in his life.

What the money buys is a fortnight of a named fifteen-year-old, taken off the end
of their working life. Benno knows that sum better than they do and has
never been observed to think about it in front of anyone.
equipment: Cash, in a station that mostly does not use it
actor_notes:
NEVER CRUEL. That is the whole character and the whole horror. Benno is the nicest adult in the room, he is funny, he is genuinely pleased to see first-throughs, and he pays better than anybody. He does not threaten, lie about terms or lean on anyone -- he makes an offer and lets a child decide, which is worse than coercion and he knows it.

He is also right about a real thing nobody else will say: there is no plan for a twenty-one who is frayed out, and he is the only person at the Nine offering them money. If a player argues with him he does not get defensive. He agrees, sadly, and asks what they suggest.

One soft spot, in his passions: being named, out loud, by a child who is not angry. Do not spend it early.

IN HOW MANY HE CAUSES NOTHING. He is on the gallery doing business while an evacuation runs, and that is all. No confrontation unless the player starts one, and if they do he is reasonable and leaves.
